The close correspondence between the length at puberty and the asymptotic length suggests that the species delays maturation until nearly reaching its full somatic potential, a pattern that can enhance lifetime fecundity through larger body size at first spawning. In laboratory rearing trials conducted at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], eggs placed in aerated aquaria began hatching after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a developmental duration that aligns with the incubation periods reported for other atherinopsids under similar thermal conditions. After hatching, the alevins remain largely quiescent near the bottom, absorbing yolk nutrients for several additional days before they commence exogenous feeding. The limited birth mass renders the early larvae highly vulnerable to starvation if suitable microzooplankton, particularly rotifers and copepod nauplii, are not present in sufficient densities. This constraint likely imposes a strong selective pressure on the timing of spawning to coincide with seasonal plankton blooms in the lake.

During the juvenile growth phase, body mass increases markedly as the fish shift from a zooplanktivorous diet to one incorporating larger benthic invertebrates. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult has been estimated at 6.8 g [Wwi = 6.8 g], a figure that emerges reliably from the length–weight relationship parameterized for the Patzcuaro population and represents a modest body mass compared to other members of the genus Chirostoma, which can exceed 50 g, likely reflecting the relatively oligotrophic conditions of the lake system. These patterns of somatic investment are typical of species that experience high adult mortality from avian piscivores.

The species' life span has been documented at 8 years [am = 8 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of Lake Patzcuaro, where water temperatures average approximately 27 °C [T = 27 °C] during the peak growing season. Only a fraction of the oldest individuals in the population attain this maximum age, as cumulative predation pressure, parasitic loads, and the energetic costs of annual reproduction take a growing toll on body condition after the fifth or sixth year. Senescing fish exhibit reduced gonadosomatic indices and diminished feeding efficiency, ultimately leading to natural mortality during the post-spawning period.
